newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Gore holds private talks with S. Korea's Kim.
newsitem.headline: Gore holds private talks with S. Korea's Kim.

text.p: U.S. Vice-President Al Gore held private talks on Saturday with South Korean President Kim Young-sam as the United States searched for a way to convince North Korea to join four-nation peace talks.
"These discussions take place at a very important time," Gore told Kim at the start of the talks at the presidential Blue House.
Gore said "the meetings I have had here ... have been very productive," but he did not elaborate while journalists were in the ornate meeting room.
Kim told Gore "we are delighted to have you here" but avoided any reference to the substance of the visit.

According to the U.S. vice-president's announced schedule, both men had planned to make statements following their talks, but that was cancelled "at the request of the South Koreans", said Ginny Terazano, Gore's press secretary.

The United States has been trying to convince North Korea to accept a proposal for four-way talks between North and South Korea, the United States and China that was proposed by U.S. President Bill Clinton and Kim in April.

The four-way talks would be aimed initially at securing a lasting peace to replace the armistice that ended the 1950-1953 Korean War, which the United States believes would serve as a springboard for ending tensions on the peninsula.
After his talks on Saturday with Kim, Gore was to visit the Demilitarized Zone separating the North and South and meet some of the 37,000 U.S. troops stationed in South Korea.
Gore, who spent five days in China before arriving in Korea on Friday, discussed the talks during his meetings with Chinese President Jiang Zemin, U.S. officials said.

According to officials in Seoul, Pyongyang has made its first formal response to the call for talks by insisting the United States and South Korea promise first to supply it with substantial food aid.

North Korea, devastated by two consecutive years of floods, has been suffering from severe food shortages, according to international relief experts. Seoul officials say that by linking food aid to the talks, Pyongyang had revealed its desperation.
Washington and Seoul have been cool to accepting preconditions for the talks, but both governments say they are sympathetic to North Korea's humanitarian needs.
According to a senior U.S. official involved in Gore's talks with Kim, "The United States and South Korea are not willing to have a precondition for entry into four-party talks".
He said, however, that North Korea had been told if it participated in the talks "there will be a great deal of goodwill ... good things will happen."
The official, noting that the United States had supplied humanitarian aid to the North, said additional supplies could be sent once talks began.
While Gore was in South Korea, a five-member delegation of U.S. senators, led by Ted Stevens, the chairman of the Senate Approprations Committee, was in Pyongyang for talks.

The delegation met Kim before departing on their mission. Accompanying Stevens were Republicans Pete Domenici of New Mexico, Thad Cochran of Mississippi, Pat Roberts of Kansas and Democrat Daniel Inouye of Hawaii.
